seo_title: Why Xactimate Estimates Differ by ZIP Code in Texas
meta_description: Why Xactimate estimates differ by ZIP code, how Texas regional price lists work, and how to spot pricing errors on your claim.
h1: Why Xactimate Estimates Differ by ZIP Code
primary_keyword: Xactimate estimates differ by ZIP code
excerpt: Xactimate prices repairs from regional price lists tied to your ZIP code. Learn how local labor, materials, and storms change estimates and how to catch pricing errors.
key_takeaways: Xactimate uses regional price lists selected by ZIP code and month.
Labor, materials, and contractor costs vary widely across Texas markets.
Post-storm demand can push real costs above software pricing.
Check the price list name and date first, then separate pricing gaps from scope gaps.
body_html:
Xactimate estimates differ by ZIP code because the software prices every line item from regional price lists built on local labor rates, material costs, and market conditions. The same roof or drywall repair can cost noticeably more in one Texas market than another, and an estimate run on the wrong ZIP code or outdated price list will be wrong.

Two homeowners with nearly identical hail damage sometimes compare insurance estimates and find meaningfully different totals. That is not necessarily an error. Xactimate is designed to reflect what repairs cost where the property sits. But pricing is also a common source of claim disputes, especially after big storms, when real-world costs move faster than software databases.

This guide explains how Xactimate pricing works, why ZIP codes matter, the Texas factors that drive local costs, and how to spot a pricing problem on your estimate.

What Is Xactimate?

Xactimate is estimating software widely used by insurance carriers, independent adjusters, public adjusters, contractors, and appraisers to price property damage repairs. An estimator enters the scope (each item of work with its quantity), and Xactimate applies unit prices for labor, materials, and equipment from a selected price list.

Insurers rely on it because it creates consistent, itemized estimates that are easy to review and compare. Its pricing is only as accurate as the price list selected and the scope entered. If you want the basics of Texas pricing, start with how Xactimate pricing works in Texas.

How Do Xactimate Price Lists Work?

Xactimate divides the country into pricing regions. Each region has its own price list, and the property's ZIP code determines which region applies. Price lists are researched and published on a recurring basis, typically monthly, so an estimate also reflects the month and year selected.

Each unit price is built from components:

  • Labor rates for the specific trade, such as roofer, drywall installer, painter, or electrician
  • Material costs for the specified product
  • Equipment charges where applicable
  • Labor minimums and small-job adjustments for very limited work

Overhead and profit, sales tax, and depreciation are applied separately in the estimate summary. Because the pricing is regional and time-specific, the price list name and date shown on an estimate are two of the first things worth checking.

Why Do ZIP Codes Change Xactimate Pricing?

Labor costs vary by market

Wages for skilled trades differ between large metro areas and rural counties. Labor availability matters too: when local contractors are scarce, rates rise.

Material prices are not uniform

Shipping distance, supplier competition, and local demand affect what a contractor pays for shingles, drywall, lumber, and fixtures. Certain specialty materials, such as particular tile profiles or metal panels, may be harder to source in some areas.

Contractor operating costs differ

Insurance, fuel, permit fees, disposal costs, and travel time all vary by location and flow into what contractors must charge.

Tip: Look near the top of your Xactimate estimate for the price list name and date. Confirm that it matches your property's market and roughly the time of loss or repair. A mismatch is one of the easiest pricing errors to spot.

Example: How the Same Repair Prices Differently by ZIP Code

Consider an illustrative example. Two houses each need a 30-square asphalt shingle roof replaced after hail. One sits in a large metro suburb, the other in a small town a couple of hours away. The scope is identical: tear-off, felt or synthetic underlayment, shingles, starter, ridge cap, drip edge, and pipe jacks.

Even with the same quantities, the two Xactimate estimates can land at different totals because:

  • The roofer labor rate built into each price list is different.
  • Shingle and underlayment material costs reflect different supply markets.
  • Disposal, permit, and delivery costs differ by location.
  • Sales tax rates vary by city and county.

The same pattern shows up inside the house. A water loss requiring drywall, insulation, paint, and baseboard can price differently in Austin than in Lubbock because the drywall installer and painter labor rates differ. Neither estimate is wrong as long as each uses the correct local price list and a complete scope.

The lesson for homeowners: comparing your total to a neighbor's or a friend's in another city tells you very little. Compare your estimate to your own market and your own scope instead.

Texas Factors That Affect Xactimate Pricing

Texas is large enough that pricing varies considerably within the state.

Market typeExamplesTypical pricing pressures
Major metrosDallas-Fort Worth, Houston, Austin, San AntonioHigher labor demand, permitting costs, heavy post-storm competition for crews
Mid-size citiesWaco, Tyler, Lubbock, Amarillo, KilleenModerate labor rates; storms can quickly exhaust local contractor capacity
Rural and remote areasWest Texas, Hill Country, small townsTravel time, delivery charges, and limited contractor availability
Coastal areasGalveston, Corpus Christi, BeaumontWind-rated materials, windstorm inspection requirements, hurricane demand surges

Coastal properties may need windstorm-compliant materials and installation, which can change both scope and price. Properties in Houston and the coast often face these issues after tropical systems, while North Texas cities see the biggest swings after major hail events.

What Happens to Pricing After a Major Storm?

After a large hailstorm, tornado, or hurricane, thousands of property owners need the same trades at once. Contractors become scarce, materials run short, and real prices can climb quickly. Software price lists are researched over time, so they may lag behind those sudden changes.

Price list providers may account for catastrophe conditions through updated or event-adjusted pricing, but the timing and degree vary. As a result, an estimate written shortly after a storm on a pre-storm price list may understate what contractors are actually charging. That is one reason post-storm claims see so many pricing disputes. Our article on why insurance estimates are often lower covers this in more depth.

Why an Xactimate Estimate Can Still Be Wrong

  1. Wrong price list. The estimate uses a neighboring region or the wrong market.
  2. Outdated price list. The estimate uses an old month that does not reflect costs at the time of repair.
  3. Missing line items. Even perfect pricing cannot fix a scope that omits items. See common Xactimate line items missing from roof claims.
  4. Wrong material selection. A lower-grade shingle, carpet, or cabinet is chosen than what was actually installed.
  5. Unique property conditions. Steep or tall roofs, limited access, and historic or custom materials may need adjustments the default line item does not include.
  6. Overhead and profit omitted on jobs that require a general contractor to coordinate multiple trades.

Pricing problem or scope problem?

When an insurance estimate and a contractor bid differ, separate the two. A pricing difference means both agree on the work but disagree on the cost per unit. A scope difference means they disagree on what work is needed. Scope differences are usually larger and more common. Our comparison of Xactimate vs contractor estimates explains how to tell them apart.

How Insurance Appraisers Evaluate Pricing Disputes

In an insurance appraisal, pricing is part of the amount of loss, so it is squarely within the appraisers' authority. A thorough appraiser will:

  • Confirm the correct price list region and date for the property and repair timeline
  • Compare software pricing with documented local contractor pricing
  • Check material grades and specifications against what was installed
  • Look for missing adjustments, such as steep and high roof charges or labor minimums
  • Evaluate whether overhead and profit is warranted

Joseph Dittman writes both Xactimate and Symbility estimates and has negotiated pricing with carrier adjusters across Texas. You can learn more about our Xactimate estimate services and Symbility estimate services, since some carriers price claims in Symbility rather than Xactimate.

Signs You Should Question Your Estimate's Pricing

  • No contractor will match it. If several licensed local contractors say they cannot do the work for the insurer's unit prices, pricing may be part of the problem.
  • The price list date is old. An estimate written months after the storm on an earlier price list deserves a second look.
  • Labor looks unusually low for specialized work such as steep roofs, tile, metal, or custom millwork.
  • Material grades do not match what was installed, for example, a three-tab shingle priced for a laminated roof.
  • Market conditions changed sharply after a widespread storm, and supplier quotes back that up.

One sign alone does not prove the estimate is wrong, but several together usually justify asking the adjuster for an explanation and a revised estimate.

Next Steps If You Disagree With Your Estimate's Pricing

ZIP code pricing is legitimate, but it is not automatically correct. Before you accept or reject an estimate, work through these steps in order so you know exactly what you are disputing and why.

  1. Request the full estimate, including the price list name and date.
  2. Ask the adjuster to explain the price list choice and any unusual unit prices.
  3. Get local itemized estimates from licensed contractors.
  4. Document market conditions, such as supplier quotes and contractor availability after the storm.
  5. Consider appraisal if the insurer agrees the loss is covered but refuses to adjust pricing.

When pricing and scope problems combine, the difference on a roof or interior claim can be substantial. Keep every estimate version, note the price list on each, and put your questions to the adjuster in writing so there is a clear record if the dispute moves to appraisal. faqs.q: How often are Xactimate price lists updated?
faqs.a: Xactimate price lists are generally researched and released on a recurring basis, typically monthly, for each pricing region. Every estimate shows which price list and date it used. If an estimate uses an older price list than the time of loss or repair, ask the adjuster why, since costs can change significantly after major storms.

faqs.q: Can an adjuster use the wrong ZIP code in Xactimate?
faqs.a: It happens. An estimate might be created with a neighboring region, a default office location, or an older file. Because the ZIP code determines the price list, the wrong selection can shift unit prices across the entire estimate. Check the price list name near the top of the estimate and compare it to your property's location.

faqs.q: Why is my contractor's price higher than the Xactimate estimate?
faqs.a: Contractors price jobs based on their actual labor, material, overhead, and scheduling costs, while Xactimate uses regional averages. After a major storm, real costs can rise faster than price lists update. The gap can also come from scope differences. Compare the estimates line by line to see whether the difference is price or missing work.

faqs.q: Can appraisal fix Xactimate pricing disputes?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Pricing is part of the amount of loss, which is what appraisal decides. Each side's appraiser can present local pricing evidence, correct price list selections, and missing adjustments. If the two appraisers cannot agree, an umpire resolves the difference, and an award signed by two of the three is generally binding.
